inputs.need:
I coordinate the inclusion health social work team at a 480-bed inner-city hospital. About 900 admissions a year are of people experiencing homelessness, and since 2024 our social workers can refer patients directly to the city's housing-first programme, which offers a permanent tenancy with intensive support without requiring sobriety or treatment first. Referrals from the hospital have been uneven: we referred 142 people in 2025, but social workers differ a lot in how often they refer, many referrals were declined as incomplete, and we do not know how many referred patients were housed or what happened to their hospital use afterwards.

I would like a mixed methods study. The quantitative part would follow everyone referred from the hospital in 2024 and 2025: how many were housed within six months, what made housing more likely, and how their emergency department visits and readmissions in the following year compare with eligible patients who were not referred. The qualitative part would talk with social workers, housing-first staff and people who were referred about what helps or blocks a referral and what happens after it. We want both parts to shape a referral pathway the hospital can adopt.

The housing-first provider holds the tenancy outcomes and has not yet agreed to share them: their board rejected our first data-sharing proposal in August because it named no data custodian. Our research ethics board approved the protocol outline on 1 September, on condition that no tenancy data are used until a data-sharing agreement is signed. I need help with the comparison group, sample sizes for both parts, and how to handle consent and trust with people who have been let down by services before.
inputs.constraints: Existing social work staff plus one peer researcher paid by the hour; hospital data from 2024 and 2025; tenancy outcomes only through a signed data-sharing agreement; a pathway proposal due to the hospital executive in September 2027.
localFacts: The social work team referred 142 inpatients to the city housing-first programme in 2025.
The research ethics board approved the protocol outline on 2026-09-01 (REB-2026-188), on condition that tenancy data are not used before a data-sharing agreement is signed.
The housing-first provider's board rejected the first data-sharing proposal on 2026-08-19 because no data custodian was named.
The hospital's inclusion health budget can pay a peer researcher with lived experience of homelessness for 200 hours.

records.title: Hospital-initiated referral to housing first and subsequent emergency department use: a matched comparison
records.authors: Mbeki-Carlsson T, Obi-Fairweather L, Soto-Lindqvist A
records.abstract: We compared 310 inpatients experiencing homelessness who were referred from hospital to a housing-first programme with 620 eligible inpatients who were not referred, matched on age, sex, number of admissions in the previous year and primary diagnosis group. Fifty-eight percent of referred patients were housed within six months. In the following year, referred patients made 6.1 emergency department visits per person against 8.4 among comparison patients, and had fewer emergency readmissions. Referred patients were more often known to the social work team before admission, so engagement with services may explain part of the difference.

records.title: Referral pathways from acute hospitals to housing-first programmes: an interview study with social workers and housing staff
records.abstract: We interviewed 21 hospital social workers and 14 housing-first staff in two cities about referrals made during a hospital admission. Referrals failed most often because identity documents or income details were missing, because the patient was discharged before the housing team could meet them, or because housing staff could not reach the patient after discharge. Social workers who knew a named housing worker referred more often and more completely. Both groups asked for a shared referral form, an agreed contact after discharge and a way for housing staff to visit the ward.

records.title: Housing-first programme outcomes by referral source: annual report of a city programme
records.venue: City Housing First Partnership annual reports
records.abstract: This annual report describes 1,020 referrals to a city housing-first programme. Referrals from hospitals were accepted less often than referrals from street outreach teams (41 against 63 percent), mainly because hospital referral forms were incomplete or the person could not be contacted after discharge. Among people who were housed, tenancy sustainment at 12 months was 81 percent and did not differ by referral source. The report gives no information on health service use and does not describe how acceptance decisions were made.

records.title: Referral selection in observational evaluations of housing programmes: eligible non-referred comparators and negative control outcomes
records.venue: Methods in Health and Housing Research
records.abstract: People referred to housing programmes differ from those who are not referred in engagement, health and support, so simple comparisons overstate benefits. Using two linked datasets, we compared strategies for choosing a comparison group. Eligible non-referred people matched on previous service use and weighted by propensity scores gave estimates closer to those from a randomised evaluation than unmatched comparisons. A negative control outcome, planned outpatient attendance, helped detect residual confounding by engagement. We recommend defining eligibility identically for both groups and measuring engagement before the index admission.

records.title: Trust, consent and data linkage with people experiencing homelessness: a participatory study
records.authors: Osei-Brennan M, Castellanos-Holm D, Tanaka-Mwangi F
records.abstract: Peer researchers with lived experience of homelessness led group discussions with 46 people about taking part in research that links health and housing data. Most were willing to allow linkage if they could decide what was linked, if data would never be shared with police, immigration or benefits agencies, and if results came back to them. Participation was higher when a peer researcher explained the study and when a small payment was offered for interviews. People described earlier research that had taken their stories and given nothing back. The authors recommend layered consent and a community advisory group.

response.synthesis: Five retrieved records, a small yield, appraised at abstract level. One matched comparison suggests fewer emergency visits after hospital referral to housing first, with engagement as a likely confounder; a methods paper shows how eligible non-referred comparators and a negative control outcome reduce that bias. Hospital referrals are accepted less often than outreach referrals because of incomplete forms and lost contact, and staff describe missing documents and early discharge as the main barriers. People experiencing homelessness will accept data linkage under clear conditions of control and non-disclosure.
response.gradeRationale: One observational comparison and a programme report for outcomes, with consistent qualitative and methods evidence; confounding by engagement and indirectness to this hospital lower certainty. Low certainty for effects on hospital use; moderate confidence in the referral barriers.

response.reading: A referral works only if it is complete, reaches a named housing worker before discharge and survives the first days after discharge; each failure point is visible in either hospital or provider data, but not both. response.sampleSize: About 260 referred inpatients in 2024 and 2025: with about half housed, the 95 percent confidence interval for the proportion housed is about plus or minus 6 percentage points, and about 130 housed patients allow about 10 predictors of housing at 13 events per predictor. Qualitative sampling follows information power: 12 to 15 referred people and 18 staff.

response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people experiencing homelessness carry disadvantage across place, income, social capital and often disability; women leaving violence, young people leaving care and people from racialised communities may meet different barriers. response.effectiveness: The study succeeds if it produces a referral pathway that raises complete referrals and housing within six months.
response.efficiency: Uses existing staff and data; the peer researcher's time is the main cost.
response.costs: Peer researcher at 200 hours and participant payments from the inclusion health budget.
response.grants: None needed for this study; the pathway could later be evaluated with external funding.
response.partnerships: The housing-first provider, a community advisory group of people with lived experience, the emergency department, and the city's homelessness services.

response.limitations: Confounding by engagement; interview sample may over-represent people who were housed; two years of referrals from one hospital.
response.summary: Layered consent, peer-led interviews, strict non-disclosure, and an unmet data-sharing gate.
